lines.text: Meera built semantic search over five question papers. It compares her query with every stored vector, and it's instant.
Now add every paper from every department, for ten years. Millions of vectors, and every single search checks them all.
And it all lives in memory, gone when the script stops.
A vector database fixes that with an index. Picture every vector as a point, linked to a handful of its nearest neighbours.
A search starts at one point, hops to whichever neighbour is closer to the query, and repeats. Most points are never touched.
The catch: it's approximate. You give up a tiny bit of accuracy for a very large gain in speed.
Each vector is stored on disk with its text and metadata: subject, year, page.
So Meera can filter to DSA papers since twenty twenty-two, and then search by meaning inside that filter.
Every result comes back with its source, so she knows which paper and which page.
To start, use Chroma: a few lines of Python, and your database is a folder on your laptop.
In a real app, PG vector keeps the vectors inside Postgres, right next to your normal tables.
So the line to remember: embed once, store with metadata, and let the index find the neighbours.
